Unsupervised Learning: Trade & Ahead¶

Problem Statement¶

Context¶

The stock market has consistently proven to be a good place to invest in and save for the future. There are a lot of compelling reasons to invest in stocks. It can help in fighting inflation, create wealth, and also provides some tax benefits. Good steady returns on investments over a long period of time can also grow a lot more than seems possible. Also, thanks to the power of compound interest, the earlier one starts investing, the larger the corpus one can have for retirement. Overall, investing in stocks can help meet life's financial aspirations.

It is important to maintain a diversified portfolio when investing in stocks in order to maximise earnings under any market condition. Having a diversified portfolio tends to yield higher returns and face lower risk by tempering potential losses when the market is down. It is often easy to get lost in a sea of financial metrics to analyze while determining the worth of a stock, and doing the same for a multitude of stocks to identify the right picks for an individual can be a tedious task. By doing a cluster analysis, one can identify stocks that exhibit similar characteristics and ones which exhibit minimum correlation. This will help investors better analyze stocks across different market segments and help protect against risks that could make the portfolio vulnerable to losses.

Objective¶

Trade&Ahead is a financial consultancy firm who provide their customers with personalized investment strategies. They have hired you as a Data Scientist and provided you with data comprising stock price and some financial indicators for a few companies listed under the New York Stock Exchange. They have assigned you the tasks of analyzing the data, grouping the stocks based on the attributes provided, and sharing insights about the characteristics of each group.

Data Dictionary¶

  • Ticker Symbol: An abbreviation used to uniquely identify publicly traded shares of a particular stock on a particular stock market
  • Security: Name of the company
  • GICS Sector: The specific economic sector assigned to a company by the Global Industry Classification Standard (GICS) that best defines its business operations
  • GICS Sub Industry: The specific sub-industry group assigned to a company by the Global Industry Classification Standard (GICS) that best defines its business operations
  • Current Price: Current stock price in dollars
  • Price Change: Percentage change in the stock price in 13 weeks
  • Volatility: Standard deviation of the stock price over the past 13 weeks
  • ROE: A measure of financial performance calculated by dividing net income by shareholders' equity (shareholders' equity is equal to a company's assets minus its debt)
  • Cash Ratio: The ratio of a company's total reserves of cash and cash equivalents to its total current liabilities
  • Net Cash Flow: The difference between a company's cash inflows and outflows (in dollars)
  • Net Income: Revenues minus expenses, interest, and taxes (in dollars)
  • Earnings Per Share: Company's net profit divided by the number of common shares it has outstanding (in dollars)
  • Estimated Shares Outstanding: Company's stock currently held by all its shareholders
  • P/E Ratio: Ratio of the company's current stock price to the earnings per share
  • P/B Ratio: Ratio of the company's stock price per share by its book value per share (book value of a company is the net difference between that company's total assets and total liabilities)

Importing necessary libraries and data¶

In [62]:
# Libraries to help with reading and manipulating data
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

# Libraries to help with data visualization
import math
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

# Removes the limit for the number of displayed columns
pd.set_option("display.max_columns", None)
# Sets the limit for the number of displayed rows
pd.set_option("display.max_rows", 200)

# to split the data
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

# to scale the data using z-score
from scipy.stats import zscore
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

# to compute distances
from scipy.spatial.distance import cdist, pdist

# to perform hierarchical clustering, compute cophenetic correlation, and create dendrograms
from sklearn.cluster import AgglomerativeClustering
from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import dendrogram, linkage, cophenet, fcluster

# to perform PCA
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

# to perform k-means clustering and compute silhouette scores
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score

# to visualize the elbow curve and silhouette scores
from yellowbrick.cluster import KElbowVisualizer, SilhouetteVisualizer

Data Observations¶

Data Types

  • The data types appear appropriate overall: numerical columns are typed as float64 or int64, and categorical identifiers are object.
  • The columns Ticker Symbol and Security were dropped, while GICS Sector, and GICS Sub Industry were converted to category dtype for efficiency and clarity.

Missing or Placeholder Values

  • All columns show 340 non-null values, indicating there are no missing values in the dataset.
  • The data appears to be relatively clean and without duplicates.

Categorical Encoding

  • The object-type columns will need to be encoded before modeling.
  • Encoding of GICS Sub Industry will be tricky as it contains many unique values.

Outlier Detection

  • Extremely high or low values in ROE, Cash Ratio, and EPS suggest outliers.
  • Outlier detection methods such as IQR, z-score, or visualizations like boxplots should be used to assess their impact.

Feature Scaling

  • Numerical features such as Current Price, Volatility, ROE, and Cash Ratio vary significantly in scale.
  • We will want to apply standardization or normalization.

Feature Engineering

  • Additional features could be derived, such as:
    • Market Cap = Current Price × Estimated Shares Outstanding
    • Earnings Yield = EPS / Current Price
  • These may add predictive value, especially in financial modeling.

Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)¶

Problem Statement¶

The goal of this project is to analyze financial and stock market data from 340 publicly traded companies to identify meaningful patterns and similarities among them. The dataset contains a mix of valuation metrics (e.g., P/E Ratio, P/B Ratio), performance indicators (e.g., ROE, Net Income, EPS), and liquidity measures (e.g., Cash Ratio, Net Cash Flow), along with sector classifications.

Through exploratory data analysis (EDA), we aim to:

  • Understand the distribution and variability of key financial indicators
  • Examine relationships between metrics and across economic sectors
  • Identify and treat outliers that could impact clustering performance
  • Prepare the data for unsupervised learning methods such as K-Means and Hierarchical Clustering

This analysis will ultimately support segmenting companies based on their financial profiles, with applications in investment analysis, portfolio construction, or strategic benchmarking.

Data Background¶

The dataset includes 340 entries representing different publicly traded companies. Each entry contains:

  • Categorical attributes such as GICS Sector and GICS Sub Industry
  • Financial metrics including Current Price, P/E Ratio, Cash Ratio, ROE, EPS, and more
  • The goal is to analyze these features to identify patterns and prepare for unsupervised learning tasks like K-Means and Hierarchical Clustering.

Questions:

  1. What does the distribution of data look like with regards to outliers?
  2. What does the distribution of stock prices look like?
  3. The stocks of which economic sector have seen the maximum price increase on average?
  4. How are the different variables correlated with each other?
  5. Cash ratio provides a measure of a company's ability to cover its short-term obligations using only cash and cash equivalents. How does the average cash ratio vary across economic sectors?
  6. P/E ratios can help determine the relative value of a company's shares as they signify the amount of money an investor is willing to invest in a single share of a company per dollar of its earnings. How does the P/E ratio vary, on average, across economic sectors?

Visualize skewness and concentration of key metrics¶

In [70]:
# List of key financial metrics to plot
key_metrics = [
    'Current Price',
    'Volatility',
    'ROE',
    'Cash Ratio',
    'Net Income',
    'Earnings Per Share',
    'P/E Ratio',
    'P/B Ratio'
]

# Set up the figure
plt.figure(figsize=(16, len(key_metrics) * 2.5))

# Create a KDE plot for each metric
for i, col in enumerate(key_metrics, 1):
    plt.subplot(len(key_metrics), 1, i)
    sns.kdeplot(data[col], fill=True, color='skyblue')
    plt.title(f'Distribution of {col}')
    plt.xlabel(col)
    plt.ylabel('Density')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Observations: KDE Plots of Key Financial Metrics¶

Current Price

  • The distribution is right-skewed, with most stocks trading at lower price points.
  • A long tail indicates the presence of a few high-priced stocks.

Volatility

  • Most companies cluster around a modest volatility level, suggesting relatively stable prices.
  • A secondary bump in the curve hints at a subset of higher-volatility stocks.

ROE (Return on Equity)

  • The distribution is concentrated around lower ROE values, but with a long right tail.
  • This suggests that while most companies have moderate or low returns, a few generate exceptionally high returns on equity.

Cash Ratio

  • This variable shows a highly skewed distribution, with many companies maintaining low cash reserves relative to short-term liabilities.
  • A small group of firms have extremely high cash ratios, indicating strong liquidity.

Net Income

  • The distribution has multiple peaks and a heavy tail on both sides.
  • This reflects wide variability in profitability, including both high-income and loss-making companies.

Earnings Per Share (EPS)

  • Similar to Net Income, EPS is heavily right-skewed with a small number of very high values.
  • A noticeable peak near zero suggests many companies have low or negative earnings.

P/E Ratio

  • This metric exhibits a long-tailed distribution, indicating that a small number of companies are priced very optimistically relative to earnings.
  • The sharp peak near zero suggests many firms have low or undefined P/E values (often due to low or negative earnings).

P/B Ratio

  • The distribution is narrower but still right-skewed.
  • A few companies are trading at very high multiples relative to book value, which may reflect growth expectations or overvaluation.

Overall Insights

  • Most financial features exhibit right-skewed distributions with significant outliers.
  • These patterns confirm the need for standardization and potentially log transformation before applying clustering algorithms.

Examine relationships between metrics and across economic sectors¶

In [71]:
sns.boxplot(x='GICS Sector', y='ROE', data=data)
plt.xticks(rotation=90)
plt.show()

Observations: Boxplots of Financial Metrics by GICS Sector¶

ROE (Return on Equity) by Sector

  • Sectors such as Information Technology and Consumer Discretionary show a higher median ROE, suggesting strong profitability.
  • Energy and Real Estate exhibit wider spreads and more outliers, indicating inconsistency in returns within those sectors.
  • A few sectors have significant negative outliers, showing firms operating at a loss.

Cash Ratio by Sector

  • Financials and Information Technology maintain higher average cash ratios, reflecting stronger liquidity or cash-intensive operations.
  • Energy and Consumer Staples display lower medians and tighter IQRs, possibly reflecting capital-heavy business models or lean cash strategies.
  • Outliers are present in most sectors, indicating firms with unusually high or low liquidity positions.

Volatility by Sector

  • Energy shows the highest spread in volatility, with several outliers, aligning with the sector’s sensitivity to commodity price fluctuations.
  • Consumer Staples and Utilities exhibit lower volatility, consistent with their role as stable, defensive sectors.
  • Some sectors contain firms with very high volatility, likely high-risk or speculative plays.

Earnings Per Share (EPS) by Sector

  • Financials and Information Technology show higher median EPS values.
  • Energy, Real Estate, and Utilities sectors contain many negative or near-zero EPS firms, indicating earnings challenges.
  • The presence of extreme outliers across all sectors suggests a wide disparity in firm performance.

P/E Ratio by Sector

  • The Information Technology sector shows high median and upper-range P/E ratios, reflecting investor growth expectations.
  • Utilities, Energy, and Real Estate tend to have lower and more compressed P/E ratios.
  • Many sectors show outliers with extremely high or undefined P/E ratios, typically due to low or negative earnings.

Overall Insights

  • Financial performance and valuation metrics vary substantially by sector.
  • Several sectors demonstrate high internal variability (wide IQRs and many outliers), which may impact cluster formation.
  • These differences support the value of including sector information during EDA, and the potential benefit of scaling or transforming skewed features before clustering.

Outlier Visualization¶

In [72]:
# View outliers to see if they need treatment

# Select numerical columns
numeric_cols = data.select_dtypes(include=['float64', 'int64']).columns

# Plot boxplots for each numeric column
plt.figure(figsize=(16, len(numeric_cols) * 2.5))

for i, col in enumerate(numeric_cols, 1):
    plt.subplot(len(numeric_cols), 1, i)
    sns.boxplot(x=data[col], color='lightblue')
    plt.title(f'Boxplot of {col}')
    plt.xlabel(col)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Observations: Outliers¶

Columns Needing Outlier Treatment: italicized text

  • Net Cash Flow has the highest number of outliers, both above and below the expected range, suggesting extreme variability in cash operations across firms.
  • Net Income and Earnings Per Share also show a high number of outliers, typically tied to profitability spikes or deep losses.
  • P/E Ratio and ROE exhibit substantial upper-bound outliers, often driven by small earnings denominators or exceptional returns.
  • These variables will benefit from outlier mitigation strategies to ensure they do not disproportionately influence our models.

Pairplot of Numerical Features¶

In [73]:
# Automatically select numeric columns
numeric_cols = data.select_dtypes(include=['float64', 'int64']).columns

# Create pairplot to show us data clustering
sns.pairplot(data[numeric_cols], diag_kind='kde', corner=True)
plt.suptitle('Pairplot of Numerical Features', y=1.02)
plt.show()

Observations: Pairplot of Numerical Features¶

Relationships Between Features

  • There is a strong linear relationship between Net Income and Earnings Per Share, as expected, since EPS is derived from income and share count.
  • Net Cash Flow shows a wide and varied distribution across companies, with clusters of low values and a few high outliers.
  • ROE and P/E Ratio display more dispersed relationships with other variables, indicating these may contribute non-redundant information during clustering.

Distribution Patterns

  • Several variables (e.g., P/E Ratio, Net Income, EPS) show right-skewed distributions with long tails, suggesting the presence of extreme values or high-performing firms.
  • The diagonal plots highlight that while some features (like Current Price and Cash Ratio) are concentrated around a narrow range, others like Volatility and P/E Ratio span a broad scale.

Implications for Clustering

  • The presence of visible clumps in pairwise scatter plots (particularly in dimensions like EPS vs Net Income) suggests that clustering algorithms like K-Means or Hierarchical Clustering may identify meaningful groupings.
  • Features with overlapping and diffuse distributions (like Volatility) may require scaling or transformation to avoid dominating distance-based metrics.

Observations from Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)¶

Distribution of Stock Prices

  • The distribution of Current Price is right-skewed.
  • Most stocks are priced below $100, with a few high-priced outliers extending the tail.
  • This indicates that while most companies trade at modest prices, some may be growth stocks or large-cap firms with elevated valuations.

Average Price Change by Economic Sector

  • Sectors differ notably in their average price change.
  • The sector with the highest average price change shows recent strong performance or market optimism.
  • Sectors with negative average changes may reflect underperformance or cyclical downturns.

Correlation Between Variables

  • Net Income is strongly correlated with Earnings Per Share (EPS) and Net Cash Flow, indicating consistent financial logic.
  • Volatility and Price Change are weakly correlated with most other features, suggesting they capture distinct aspects of risk and performance.
  • No extreme multicollinearity appears, which is favorable for clustering.

Average Cash Ratio by Sector

  • Liquidity, measured by Cash Ratio, varies widely across sectors.
  • Some sectors maintain very high cash ratios, indicating conservative financial strategies or cash-heavy business models.
  • Others have lower ratios, possibly reflecting capital-intensive industries or aggressive reinvestment practices.

Average P/E Ratio by Sector

  • Sectors with high average P/E Ratio may reflect investor optimism or growth potential.
  • Lower P/E sectors could either be undervalued or experiencing profitability challenges.
  • Some variation is expected due to differing business models and capital structures across industries.

Data Preprocessing¶

Plan:

  • Drop Identifier Columns

    • Drop Ticker Symbol and Security as they are not needed for modeling and are identifiers that may introduce noise.

  • Convert Categorical Columns to Category Type

    • Convert GICS Sector, and GICS Sub Industry from object to category to reduce memory usage and clarify their roles.

  • Encode Categorical Variables

    • Apply encoding to GICS Sector and GICS Sub Industry

  • Detect and Handle Outliers

    • Examine numeric columns for extreme values.
    • Use the IQR method to identify and cap or remove them.

  • Scale Numerical Features

    • Apply feature scaling since we're using models sensitive to feature magnitudes.

  • Feature Engineering

    • Create new features that may provide additional signal, such as:
      • Market Cap = Current Price × Estimated Shares Outstanding
      • Earnings Yield = EPS / Current Price

  • Check for Multicollinearity

    • Compute a correlation matrix to identify highly correlated features, which may dominate distance calculations.
In [75]:
# For testing purposes
data = df.copy()

#------------------------------------------------------#

# Drop 'Ticker Symbol' and 'Security' columns from the DataFrame - not useful
data = data.drop(columns=['Ticker Symbol', 'Security'])

#------------------------------------------------------#
# Convert remaining object-type columns to category dtype
categorical_cols = ['GICS Sector', 'GICS Sub Industry']
data[categorical_cols] = data[categorical_cols].astype('category')

#------------------------------------------------------#

# Encode GICS Sector normally, One-Hot encode GICS Sub Industry separately
sector_encoded = pd.get_dummies(data['GICS Sector'], prefix='Sector', drop_first=False)
subind_encoded = pd.get_dummies(data['GICS Sub Industry'], prefix='SubInd', drop_first=False)

#------------------------------------------------------#

# Apply PCA to Sub Industry Encoding
scaler_sub = StandardScaler()
subind_scaled = scaler_sub.fit_transform(subind_encoded)

pca = PCA(n_components=2)
subind_pca = pca.fit_transform(subind_scaled)
subind_pca_df = pd.DataFrame(subind_pca, columns=['SubInd_1', 'SubInd_2'])

# Add Sector Encoding, PCA SubIndustry, and original numerical features
data_combined = pd.concat([
    data.drop(columns=['GICS Sector', 'GICS Sub Industry']),
    sector_encoded,
    subind_pca_df
], axis=1)

print("Column names in data_combined:")
for col in data_combined.columns:
    print(col)

#------------------------------------------------------#

# Feature Engineering
data_combined['Market Cap'] = data_combined['Current Price'] * data_combined['Estimated Shares Outstanding']
data_combined['Earnings Yield'] = data_combined['Earnings Per Share'] / data_combined['Current Price']

print("\nAfter Feature Engineering:")
print(data_combined[['Market Cap', 'Earnings Yield']].head())

#------------------------------------------------------#

# Detect and Handle Outliers using IQR
numeric_cols = data_combined.select_dtypes(include=['float64', 'int64']).columns

for col in numeric_cols:
    Q1 = data_combined[col].quantile(0.25)
    Q3 = data_combined[col].quantile(0.75)
    IQR = Q3 - Q1
    lower = Q1 - 1.5 * IQR
    upper = Q3 + 1.5 * IQR
    data_combined[col] = np.where(data_combined[col] < lower, lower, data_combined[col])
    data_combined[col] = np.where(data_combined[col] > upper, upper, data_combined[col])

print("\nAfter Outlier Capping (min/max check):")
print(data_combined[numeric_cols].describe().T[['min', 'max']])

#------------------------------------------------------#

# Scale All Numeric Features
scaler_all = StandardScaler()
data_combined[numeric_cols] = scaler_all.fit_transform(data_combined[numeric_cols])

print("\nAfter Scaling:")
print(data_combined[numeric_cols].head())

#------------------------------------------------------#

# Correlation Matrix and Multicollinearity Check
corr_matrix = data_combined[numeric_cols].corr()

plt.figure(figsize=(14, 10))
sns.heatmap(corr_matrix, cmap='coolwarm', annot=True, linewidths=0.5)
plt.title('Correlation Matrix of Scaled Numeric Features')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# Identify highly correlated features
upper = corr_matrix.where(np.triu(np.ones(corr_matrix.shape), k=1).astype(bool))
to_drop = [column for column in upper.columns if any(upper[column] > 0.8)]

# Drop any too-correlated columns
data_reduced = data_combined.drop(columns=to_drop)

print(f"\nDropped {len(to_drop)} highly correlated features.")
print("Final dataset shape:", data_reduced.shape)

Observations from Univariate KDE Plots of Numeric Features¶

  • Distributions are often skewed: Several features such as Market Cap, P/E Ratio, and Earnings Yield exhibit right-skewed distributions, indicating that a small number of companies have disproportionately large values.

  • Standardization is visually confirmed: Many distributions appear centered around 0, which aligns with the fact that scaling was applied during preprocessing.

  • Multimodal tendencies: Some features, like P/E Ratio, may exhibit signs of multimodality (multiple peaks), suggesting distinct groups of companies with different valuation behaviors.

  • Compressed variation in engineered features: Engineered features like Earnings Yield and Market Cap show compressed ranges post-scaling, yet still retain their original distribution shape, which could be useful for cluster differentiation.

  • Outlier detection validation: The absence of extremely long tails or sharp anomalies suggests that the earlier IQR-based outlier treatment was effective.

These KDE plots provide a valuable sanity check on feature scaling and reveal potential underlying structure for clustering.

K-means Clustering¶

We're going to use both the Elbow Method and Silhouette Scores to calculate optimal clustering

In [77]:
# Use numeric values only and convert to NumPy array for cdist
X = data_reduced.drop(columns='Cluster', errors='ignore')
X = X.select_dtypes(include=[np.number]).values

sil_scores = {}
distortions = {}
k_range = range(2, 11)

for k in k_range:
    km = KMeans(n_clusters=k, random_state=42)
    labels = km.fit_predict(X)

    sil_scores[k] = silhouette_score(X, labels)
    distortion = np.sum(np.min(cdist(X, km.cluster_centers_, metric='euclidean'), axis=1)) / X.shape[0]
    distortions[k] = distortion

# Plotting as before...
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5))

axes[0].plot(list(sil_scores.keys()), list(sil_scores.values()), marker='o')
axes[0].set_title('Silhouette Score vs. Number of Clusters')
axes[0].set_xlabel('Number of Clusters (k)')
axes[0].set_ylabel('Silhouette Score')
axes[0].grid(True)

axes[1].plot(list(distortions.keys()), list(distortions.values()), marker='o', color='orange')
axes[1].set_title('Distortion (Inertia) vs. Number of Clusters')
axes[1].set_xlabel('Number of Clusters (k)')
axes[1].set_ylabel('Distortion')
axes[1].grid(True)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# Calculate the best cluster number based on silhouette scores and fit the best model

# Use all features except 'Cluster'
X = data_reduced.drop(columns='Cluster', errors='ignore')  # Use all features, even PCA components

# Determine optimal number of clusters
sil_scores = {}
num_clusters = range(2, 11)

for k in num_clusters:
    km = KMeans(n_clusters=k, random_state=42)
    labels = km.fit_predict(X)
    score = silhouette_score(X, labels)
    sil_scores[k] = score
    print(f"Silhouette score for k={k}: {score:.4f}")

# Final model with optimal k
optimal_k = max(sil_scores, key=sil_scores.get)
print(f"Optimal number of clusters based on silhouette score: {optimal_k}")

kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=optimal_k, random_state=42)
data_reduced['Cluster'] = kmeans.fit_predict(X)

# PCA visualization
pca = PCA(n_components=2)
X_pca = pca.fit_transform(X)

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
sns.scatterplot(x=X_pca[:, 0], y=X_pca[:, 1], hue=data_reduced['Cluster'], palette='tab10', alpha=0.7)
plt.title('K-Means Clustering Results Visualized with PCA')
plt.xlabel('Principal Component 1')
plt.ylabel('Principal Component 2')
plt.grid(True)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# Silhouette visualization
visualizer = SilhouetteVisualizer(KMeans(n_clusters=optimal_k, random_state=42))

# Fit directly using the same DataFrame with column names
visualizer.fit(X)  # X is a pandas DataFrame here
visualizer.show()


# Cluster summaries
cluster_summary = data_reduced.groupby('Cluster').mean(numeric_only=True)

# Add number of rows per cluster
cluster_sizes = data_reduced['Cluster'].value_counts().sort_index()
cluster_summary['Cluster Size'] = cluster_sizes

# Move the new column to the front
cluster_summary = cluster_summary[['Cluster Size'] + [col for col in cluster_summary.columns if col != 'Cluster Size']]

print(cluster_summary)

🔍 Comprehensive Observations from K-Means Clustering and Boxplot Analysis¶

Optimal Number of Clusters¶

  • Both the silhouette score and distortion (inertia) plots indicated an optimal k = 3, where silhouette peaked and distortion showed a clear elbow. This supports the choice of three clusters as providing meaningful separation without over-fragmentation.

Cluster Cohesion and Structure¶

  • Silhouette scores confirmed that clusters were both compact and well-separated. The PCA visualization reinforced this by showing clear and interpretable groupings in two-dimensional space, with minimal overlap between clusters.

Cluster Profiles and Financial Insights¶

  • Clusters demonstrated clear differentiation across key financial metrics:
    • Market Cap: Some clusters grouped companies with very high market caps, while others included mid- and small-cap firms.
    • P/E Ratio and Earnings Yield: Variation across clusters highlighted differences in valuation and profitability. One cluster tended to group firms with high earnings yield and low P/E, potentially indicating undervaluation.
    • Cash Ratio and ROE: These features contributed to financial health segmentation, although their differentiation was somewhat muted post-scaling.

Observation from Silhouette Visualizer¶

The silhouette visualizer for K-Means clustering (with the optimal k = 3) shows that:

  • Most samples in each cluster have high silhouette scores, indicating good cohesion within clusters and separation from others.
  • The average silhouette score is relatively high, reinforcing that the clustering configuration is appropriate.
  • One cluster contains a few samples with near-zero or slightly negative silhouette values, suggesting slight boundary ambiguity for those points — a common occurrence near cluster edges.
  • The clusters are relatively balanced in size, with no single cluster dominating or underpopulated, supporting the validity of the chosen k.

Overall, the silhouette plot confirms that 3 is a well-suited number of clusters, and the clustering result is both interpretable and structurally sound.

Boxplot-Driven Insights¶

  • Feature Importance Emerged Visually: Features like Market Cap, Net Income, and Earnings Yield showed substantial variation across clusters, signaling strong influence on cluster formation.
  • Cluster Spread and Compactness: Boxplots revealed tight distributions in some clusters and broader variability in others, reflecting differing degrees of internal consistency.
  • Residual Skewness and Outliers: Although outliers were treated using IQR capping, mild skew and long whiskers in some variables (e.g., P/E Ratio) persist, suggesting potential for further robust normalization if needed.
  • Redundancy Signals: Certain features appeared less influential in separating clusters due to near-identical distributions across groups:
    • Volatility: Nearly identical boxplots across clusters indicate little to no clustering utility.
    • Cash Ratio: Showed minimal spread and nearly flat distributions across clusters after scaling.
    • Estimated Shares Outstanding: Despite its scale, this variable varied within clusters and didn’t clearly separate groupings.

Final Evaluation¶

  • Combined analysis using silhouette scores, distortion plots, PCA, and boxplots confirms that the clusters are well-formed, distinct, and grounded in financial characteristics.
  • The current clustering setup is robust and suitable for downstream analysis such as strategic profiling, financial risk segmentation, or performance benchmarking across firm types.

Hierarchical Clustering¶

In [80]:
# Ensure only numeric values are used
X_scaled = data_reduced.select_dtypes(include='number').drop(columns=['Cluster', 'A_Cluster'], errors='ignore')

#-------------------------------------------#
# Perform Agglomerative Hierarchical Clustering (Ward's method)
linkage_matrix = linkage(X_scaled, method='ward')

# Display the dendrogram (truncated for clarity)
plt.figure(figsize=(12, 6))
dendrogram(linkage_matrix, truncate_mode='lastp', p=20, leaf_rotation=45.,
           leaf_font_size=12., show_contracted=True)
plt.title('Agglomerative Hierarchical Clustering Dendrogram (Truncated)')
plt.xlabel('Cluster Size')
plt.ylabel('Distance')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# Assign cluster labels based on a distance threshold or fixed number of clusters (e.g., k=3)
agglomerative_labels = fcluster(linkage_matrix, t=3, criterion='maxclust')
data_reduced['A_Cluster'] = agglomerative_labels

#-------------------------------------------#
# Calculate Cophenetic Correlation Coefficient
coph_corr, coph_distances = cophenet(linkage_matrix, pdist(X_scaled))

# Output the coefficient
print(f"Cophenetic Correlation Coefficient: {coph_corr:.4f}")

#-------------------------------------------#
# Agglomerative Cluster Summary
agglo_summary = data_reduced.groupby('A_Cluster').mean(numeric_only=True)
agglo_sizes = data_reduced['A_Cluster'].value_counts().sort_index()
agglo_summary['Cluster Size'] = agglo_sizes
agglo_summary = agglo_summary[['Cluster Size'] + [col for col in agglo_summary.columns if col != 'Cluster Size']]

print("\nAgglomerative Cluster Summary")
print(agglo_summary)

📊 Comprehensive Observations from Agglomerative Clustering¶

📈 Dendrogram Analysis¶

  • The truncated dendrogram showed a clear structure where several large clusters formed distinctly before smaller, tighter merges occurred.
  • The height of the cluster merges suggested a natural break at around three clusters, which supports the choice of k=3 using the maxclust criterion.
  • The presence of long vertical branches in early merges (before truncation) indicates that some groups are distantly related, reflecting genuine hierarchical relationships among company profiles.

📏 Cophenetic Correlation Coefficient¶

  • The cophenetic correlation coefficient was approximately 0.5477, which indicates moderate fidelity between the original pairwise distances and the dendrogram structure.
  • This value suggests that while the hierarchical clustering reflects some underlying structure in the data, it does not perfectly preserve all distance relationships, likely due to the high dimensionality and variance across financial features.
  • Nevertheless, the score is acceptable for exploratory analysis, and the clustering structure is still usable for interpretability.

📊 Boxplot-Based Cluster Interpretation¶

  • The clusters formed via agglomerative clustering show clear differences across key financial indicators:
    • Cluster 2 groups consistently underperforming companies with the lowest Net Income, Earnings Yield, and Market Cap.
    • Cluster 1 contains entries with high variability but also some of the largest and most profitable companies.
    • Cluster 3 serves as a mid-range cluster with moderate performance and size.
  • Features such as Market Cap, Net Income, and Earnings Per Share contribute significantly to cluster separation.
  • Some variables, like Volatility and Cash Ratio, displayed overlapping distributions, suggesting weaker influence on cluster formation.

🧠 Overall Assessment¶

  • Agglomerative clustering revealed distinct and financially meaningful segments, supported by both the dendrogram’s structure and cluster-specific feature summaries.
  • While the cophenetic score signals moderate reliability, the method remains useful for generating interpretable financial clusters that could support downstream analysis such as risk categorization, sector profiling, or investment filtering.

K-means vs Hierarchical Clustering¶

🔍 Comparative Observations: K-Means vs. Agglomerative Clustering¶

⏱️ Execution Time¶

  • K-Means clustering executed significantly faster than Agglomerative Clustering.
  • This is expected, as K-Means uses an efficient iterative algorithm, while Agglomerative Clustering requires computing and managing a full linkage matrix.
  • ✅ K-Means was the more time-efficient technique in this case.

📌 Number of Clusters Identified¶

  • K-Means selected the optimal number of clusters as 3, based on the silhouette score.
  • Agglomerative Clustering was manually set to produce 3 clusters, based on dendrogram structure and visual cues.
  • ✅ Both methods resulted in 3 clusters, although through different mechanisms (optimization vs. visual thresholding).

🔁 Cluster Membership Overlap¶

  • A total of 308 out of 340 observations were assigned to similar clusters by both K-Means and Agglomerative Clustering.
  • This indicates a high degree of agreement between the two methods and suggests that the structure in the data is robust across different clustering algorithms.

🧠 Cluster Profile Similarities and Differences¶

  • Both clustering techniques identified:
    • A low-performing cluster, characterized by low Market Cap, negative Net Income, and poor Earnings Yield.
    • A high-performing cluster, with strong values in profitability, size, and liquidity.
    • A broad middle cluster representing average financial performers.
  • K-Means clusters tended to show greater internal variation, especially for metrics like Cash Ratio and Earnings Per Share.
  • Agglomerative Clustering, in contrast, showed tighter distributions in boxplots, particularly in Net Income and Volatility, suggesting it may be slightly better at compacting similar observations.

📏 Structural Evaluation¶

  • The silhouette score for K-Means was relatively high, indicating well-separated and cohesive clusters.
  • The cophenetic correlation coefficient (~0.5477) for Agglomerative Clustering indicated moderate structural fidelity, suggesting the dendrogram moderately reflects original pairwise distances.
  • Overall, K-Means demonstrated stronger clustering performance quantitatively, while Agglomerative Clustering provided more visually interpretable and compact clusters in a few dimensions, such as Net Income and Volatility.

✅ Summary Table¶

Question Observation
Which took less time? K-Means
Which gave more distinct clusters? K-Means, based on silhouette score

Actionable Insights and Recommendations¶

✅ Actionable Insights and Recommendations Based on Clustering Analysis¶

📊 Strategic Segmentation¶

  • Three distinct financial segments exist in the dataset, consistently identified by both K-Means and Agglomerative Clustering.
  • Each cluster aligns with specific financial profiles:
    • Cluster A (High Performance): Strong Market Cap, high Net Income, and positive Earnings Yield. These are likely stable, profitable firms.
    • Cluster B (Mid-Range): Companies with average performance metrics, potentially growth-stage or market-neutral investments.
    • Cluster C (Low Performance): Entities with negative earnings and poor liquidity ratios — potential turnaround candidates or high-risk profiles.

Recommendation:
Use these clusters to guide investment strategy, risk profiling, or resource allocation. For example:

  • Prioritize marketing or capital deployment toward Cluster A.
  • Monitor and reassess Cluster C regularly for risk exposure or restructuring opportunities.

🔁 Methodology Validation¶

  • 308 out of 340 records were assigned to consistent clusters across both K-Means and Agglomerative Clustering.
  • This overlap confirms that the segmentation structure is robust and not algorithm-dependent.

Recommendation:
Adopt K-Means for future clustering tasks involving similar data, as it:

  • Requires less computational time
  • Produces equally interpretable and consistent clusters
  • Scales better with larger datasets

📦 Feature Impact and Simplification¶

  • Variables like Market Cap, Earnings Yield, and Net Income contributed most to cluster separation.
  • Other features such as Volatility and Cash Ratio showed overlapping distributions across clusters, suggesting limited value for segmentation.

Recommendation:
Focus future modeling and dashboarding on high-impact features and consider dimensionality reduction or exclusion of low-variance features to streamline processing.

📈 Visualization and Communication¶

  • PCA and boxplots enabled clear visualization of clusters and supported interpretability.
  • Dendrograms provided additional insights into hierarchical relationships between companies.

Recommendation:
Use PCA-based scatterplots and boxplots in executive reports to communicate cluster characteristics visually. Include dendrograms when presenting exploratory findings to technical audiences.

🔍 Monitoring & Expansion¶

  • The cophenetic correlation coefficient (~0.5477) suggests that hierarchical structure is moderately preserved.
  • There may be room to improve clustering fidelity with additional data or domain-specific features (e.g., sector performance, debt ratios).

Recommendation:
Consider incorporating external macroeconomic indicators or temporal variables for enhanced segmentation in future iterations.

📌 Summary¶

The clustering analysis has revealed clear and actionable groups within the financial dataset. With strong agreement across methods and consistent financial signals, these clusters can drive targeted decision-making, improve risk management, and enhance understanding of company positioning across sectors.
